rationale:
Evidence: every raced design has gone off track in all 60 development trials (finish rate 0). max_error sits at the 0.06 m off-track limit, which cannot be raised within the allowed body_width range, and rms_error is about 0.03. Steering oscillation is low (0.06 to 0.17), so the robot drifts to the edge rather than jittering. Progress is what the score rewards here (250*progress plus a progress-scaled term), so each extra fraction of the course is worth about 4 points.

What the telemetry shows: iterations 0, 1 and 3 (narrow array, kd 0.05 to 0.3, speed 1.2) all stalled at about 0.04 progress on the s-bend. Dropping base_speed from 1.2 to 0.9 (iteration 5) raised s-bend progress to about 0.14, so the early sharp bend is speed-limited. Raising kd from 0.8 to 1.2 with a narrower track and lower mass (iteration 6) raised oval progress to 0.24 and the score to 69.3. Integral action (iteration 3) did not help, so ki stays 0.

Changes: (1) Keep the wide 7-sensor geometry, sensor size, mass, wheel track and wheel radius from iteration 6, so the only change is the controller and the test isolates the effect. (2) Raise kd from 1.2 to 1.6 to keep damping the overshoot on bends, since kd has been the variable that moved the score most. (3) Lower base_speed from 0.9 to 0.7, continuing the trend that cut the early-bend failure: slower entry gives the steering more time to settle. (4) Keep kp 4.5, ki 0 and last_direction line loss.

Expected result: the robot should hold the line through the first sharp bend and progress should rise above the 0.14 s-bend and 0.24 oval values seen so far. Completing the course within 3 s is unlikely at this speed; once tracking holds, a later revision should raise base_speed in steps. The main risk is that too much kd, combined with slower speed, makes the robot sluggish on the wider bends.
